tips.title: Write the multiplier first
tips.body: $+3\%$ is $\times 1.03$; $-15\%$ is $\times 0.85$. Then repeated change is just $\text{start} \times (\text{multiplier})^n$. Making the multiplier your first line of working turns every question in this topic into one calculation.

tips.title: Percentages multiply, they never add
tips.body: Up 20% then down 20% is $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$ — a **4% fall**, not no change. Up 10% twice is $1.21$, a **21%** rise. To get the overall change, multiply the multipliers and read the answer.

tips.title: After, including, in a sale means divide
tips.body: If a price is £120 **after** a 20% rise, the original is $120 \div 1.2 = £100$, not £120 minus 20%. Those three phrases tell you the number you have is the **result**, so undo the multiplier by dividing — then check forwards.

tips.title: Show the year below and the year above
tips.body: For *how many years until it exceeds…*, try values and write down **both** the year that is still short and the year that passes. The one below proves the earlier year is not enough; the one above proves the answer. One value alone proves nothing.

tips.title: A further 10% off is not 10% of the original
tips.body: "30% off, then a **further** 10% off" is $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$, so **37% off** — not 40%. The second reduction comes off the price the first one left behind, so it always saves less than it sounds.

why.matters:
Compound growth is what happens when a change is applied to the result of the last change. Each step is small and the total is not, because **the multipliers multiply**.

No amount of intuition prepares you for this. People reason about growth by adding, and the answer is always too small — sometimes by a little, often by a lot. The multiplier method is short, and being fluent with it is the difference between understanding a savings account, a mortgage or a news story about growth rates and merely reading one.

examples.title: A 10% fall and a 10% rise
examples.body:
Shares worth £1,000 drop 10%, then recover by 10%. Back where you started?

No. £1,000 falls to £900, and 10% of £900 is only £90, so you end at £990. You are £10 down.

The multipliers explain it in one line: $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$, not 1. The rise is a percentage of a smaller number than the fall was, so it can never catch up — and the order makes no difference, because multiplication does not care.

This is not a trick question. It is why a fund that loses 10% needs more than 10% to recover, why "prices fell 10% then rose 10%" is never a return to where things were, and why percentage changes should be multiplied rather than added.

examples.title: Ten years of the same 10%
examples.body:
Put £1,000 somewhere that grows 10% a year and leave it for 10 years.

Adding gives £2,000: 10% of £1,000 is £100, ten times over. Multiplying gives $£1,000 \times 1.1^{10} = £2,594$ — £594 more, because each year's growth grows too.

The shortcut worth carrying is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the percentage and you get the doubling time. Here that is 7.2 years, and the exact answer is 7.3 — close enough to do in your head, and it works for any rate.

That single number is how to judge a growth claim quickly. 10% a year sounds modest until you notice it means doubling about every 7.3 years, which is 2× in seven years and 4× in fifteen.

steps.title: The multiplier
steps.body:
Every percentage change can be done in **one multiplication**, and that is what makes repeated changes manageable.

- An increase of 3% multiplies by **1.03** — the original 100% plus 3%.
- A decrease of 15% multiplies by **0.85** — 100% minus 15%.

$$\text{increase of } p\% : \times \left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right) \qquad \text{decrease of } p\% : \times \left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)$$

That number is the **multiplier**, and finding it is always the first line of working.

The reason it matters here: to apply the change **repeatedly**, you just use the multiplier repeatedly. Five years of 3% growth is $\times 1.03$ five times, which is $\times 1.03^5$.

So the whole topic is one formula:

$$\text{final} = \text{start} \times (\text{multiplier})^n$$

steps.title: Why a rise and a fall do not cancel
steps.body:
A price goes up 20%, then down 20%. Is it back where it started?

**No.** The multipliers are $1.2$ and $0.8$, and

$$1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$$

so the price ends at **96%** of where it began — a 4% fall overall. £100 becomes £120, then 20% of £120 is £24, leaving £96.

The reason is that the two percentages are **of different amounts**. The rise was 20% of £100; the fall was 20% of £120, which is more.

This generalises, and it is the single most tested idea in the topic:

- **Percentages do not add.** A 10% rise followed by another 10% rise is $1.1 \times 1.1 = 1.21$, a **21%** rise, not 20%.
- **Multipliers multiply**, whatever order you apply them in — $1.2 \times 0.8$ and $0.8 \times 1.2$ both give $0.96$, so the order does not change the final amount.

To find the **overall percentage change**, multiply the multipliers and read the result: $0.96$ means a 4% decrease, $1.21$ means a 21% increase.

steps.title: How many years?
steps.body:
A question may give a target and ask **how long** it takes. At GCSE you find it by **trying values**, showing the two years either side of the answer.

The working must show the year that is **still below** the target and the year that **passes** it. One value alone does not prove anything.

steps.title: Going deeper: reverse percentages, and reading the question
steps.body:
**Reverse percentages.** If a price is £120 **after** a 20% increase, the original was **not** £120 minus 20%. It was

$$\frac{120}{1.2} = £100$$

Because £120 is $120\%$ of the original, you **divide by the multiplier** to undo it. Taking 20% off £120 gives £96, which is wrong — and it is wrong for exactly the same reason a rise and fall do not cancel.

The signal for a reverse percentage is the words **after**, **including**, or **in a sale**. *A coat costs £48 in a 20% sale* means £48 is 80% of the original, so the original is $48 \div 0.8 = £60$.

**Compound or simple?** Read which the question says. Simple interest pays the same amount every year, so £2000 at 3% simple gives £60 every year and £2300 after five. Compound gives £2318.55. If the question does not say, look for the word *compound* — and note that simple interest is now rare in real products.

**Answering what was asked.** Compound interest questions very often want the **interest earned**, not the final value. Subtract the original. It is one line, and it is the difference between full marks and one.

**Money to 2 decimal places.** £2318.5478… is £2318.55. Writing £2318.5 or £2318 loses the accuracy mark.

**A useful check.** For growth, the answer must be **bigger** than you started with; for decay, **smaller**. And for depreciation over several years the value should fall quickly at first and then more slowly, because each year's loss is a percentage of a smaller amount.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A percentage change is one multiplication by a **multiplier**: $+3\%$ is $\times 1.03$, $-15\%$ is $\times 0.85$.
- Repeated change: $\text{final} = \text{start} \times (\text{multiplier})^n$.
- **Compound interest** pays interest on interest, so each year's interest is larger than the last.
- £2000 at 3% for 5 years gives £2318.55, of which £318.55 is interest.
- **Simple** interest on the same money gives only £2300.
- **Depreciation** is the same with a multiplier below 1: £12000 falling 15% a year is £7369.50 after 3 years.
- **Percentages do not add.** Up 20% then down 20% is $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$: a **4% fall**, not no change.
- To find the overall change, **multiply the multipliers** and read the result.
- **How many years**: try values, and show the year **below** and the year **above** the target.
- **Reverse percentages**: *after*, *including* and *in a sale* all mean **divide** by the multiplier.
- Read whether the question wants the **final value** or the **interest earned**.
- Money is given to **2 decimal places**.

questions.solution: The multiplier for a three percent increase is one point zero three. After five years the value is two thousand times one point zero three to the power five, which is two thousand three hundred and eighteen pounds and fifty five pence to the nearest penny. The interest earned is the final value minus the amount invested, which is three hundred and eighteen pounds and fifty five pence. To find when the investment first exceeds two thousand five hundred pounds, try values either side. After seven years the value is two thousand four hundred and fifty nine pounds and seventy five pence, which is still below two thousand five hundred. After eight years the value is two thousand five hundred and thirty three pounds and fifty four pence, which is above it. Therefore the investment first exceeds two thousand five hundred pounds after eight whole years. Both values must be shown, because the one below proves that seven years is not enough and the one above proves that eight years is.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The value.** Multiplier $= 1.03$.

$$2000 \times 1.03^5 = £2318.55$$

**The interest.** Subtract what was invested — this is what the question asks for, and it is a separate mark:

$$£2318.55 - £2000 = £318.55$$

**How many years.** Try values either side:

- 7 years: $2000 \times 1.03^7 = £2459.75$ — still **below**
- 8 years: $2000 \times 1.03^8 = £2533.54$ — **above**

So it first exceeds £2500 after **8 whole years**.

Show **both** values. The one below proves 7 is not enough; the one above proves 8 is. One value alone proves nothing.

questions.prompt: A shop raises all its prices by 20%, then in a later sale reduces them by 20%. A customer says the prices are back to what they were. Explain why the customer is wrong, and find the overall percentage change.
questions.solution: The customer is wrong because the two percentages are percentages of different amounts. The increase of twenty percent is twenty percent of the original price, but the reduction of twenty percent is twenty percent of the new, higher price, and so it takes off more money than was added. Working with multipliers shows this clearly. An increase of twenty percent is a multiplier of one point two, and a decrease of twenty percent is a multiplier of nought point eight. Applying both gives one point two multiplied by nought point eight, which is nought point nine six. This means the final price is ninety six percent of the original, so overall the prices have fallen by four percent. For example, a hundred pound item rises to a hundred and twenty pounds, and twenty percent of a hundred and twenty is twenty four pounds, leaving ninety six pounds rather than the original hundred.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why the customer is wrong.** The two percentages are **of different amounts**. The rise is 20% of the **original** price; the fall is 20% of the **new, higher** price, so it removes more than was added.

**With multipliers.**

$$1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$$

The final price is **96%** of the original: an overall **4% decrease**.

**A concrete example.** £100 rises to £120. Then 20% of £120 is £24, leaving **£96** — not £100.

The general point is that percentages **multiply**, they do not add, which is why no sequence of a rise and an equal fall ever returns to the start.

examTechnique.body:
Write the multiplier down before anything else, and check whether it should be above or below 1.

Use the power for the number of years rather than multiplying repeatedly — but if you are unsure, a year-by-year table is perfectly acceptable and shows your working.

Read whether the question wants the **final value** or the **interest earned**. Subtracting the original is one line and often the difference between full marks and one.

For an overall change after two changes, multiply the multipliers and interpret the result: 0.96 is a 4% fall, 1.21 a 21% rise.

Watch for *after*, *including* and *in a sale*: those mean divide, not subtract. Always check a reverse percentage by working forwards.

Give money to 2 decimal places, and sanity check the direction — growth must go up, decay must come down.
examinerErrors: Adding percentages instead of multiplying multipliers.
Subtracting the percentage for a reverse percentage question instead of dividing.
Giving the final value when the question asked for the interest earned.
Using the simple interest method when the question says compound.
Multiplying the rate by the number of years for depreciation.
Rounding money to fewer than 2 decimal places.
Giving a decimal number of years when interest is added annually.
Showing only one trial value in a 'how many years' question.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the multiplier first and never touches a percentage again, which is why it never adds them by accident. It knows that a rise and an equal fall do not cancel, and can explain **why** — that the two percentages are of different amounts — rather than only quoting the result. It spots a reverse percentage from the wording and divides, checking forwards before moving on. For a *how many years* question it shows the values either side without being told to, because it understands that one value does not establish an answer. And it reads the last line of the question to see whether the value or the interest was wanted.
